section.title: The Glory Returns and the Altar
section.sectionRationale: The measured, empty house of chapters 40-42 now receives its purpose: the very glory that departed in stages in chapters 10-11 returns, filling the temple from the east. What sin drove out, grace brings back, and the chapter closes by consecrating the altar where atonement will again be made.
section.thesis: The glory that abandoned a defiled temple now returns to dwell with God's people forever, teaching that God's presence departs from sin but comes back to a purified and consecrated dwelling, a pattern completed when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and consummated when God Himself is the temple of the new creation.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: the glory of the LORD returning and filling the temple; God's declaration that this is the place of His throne where He will dwell forever; Ezekiel commissioned to describe the temple so Israel is ashamed and instructed; the precise measurements of the new altar; and the seven-day rite that consecrates the altar for sacrifice.

units.label: The glory returns
units.note: filling the temple from the east

verses.text: Then the man brought me back to the gate that faces east,
and I saw the {{kavod|glory}} of the God of Israel coming from the east. His voice was like the roar of many waters, and the earth shone with His glory.
The vision I saw was like the vision I had seen when He came to destroy the city and like the visions I had seen by the River Kebar. I fell facedown,
and the glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east.
Then the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple.
While the man was standing beside me, I heard someone speaking to me from inside the temple,

and He said to me, “Son of man, this is the place of My throne and the place for the soles of My feet, where I will {{shakan|dwell}} among the Israelites forever. The house of Israel will never again defile My holy name, neither they nor their kings, by their prostitution and by the funeral offerings for their kings at their deaths.

When they placed their threshold next to My threshold and their doorposts beside My doorposts, with only a wall between Me and them, they defiled My holy name by the abominations they committed. Therefore I have consumed them in My anger.
Now let them remove far from Me their prostitution and the funeral offerings for their kings, and I will dwell among them forever.

units.label: Ashamed and instructed: the law of the temple

verses.text: As for you, son of man, describe the temple to the people of Israel, so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities. Let them measure the plan,

and if they are ashamed of all they have done, then make known to them the design of the temple, its arrangement and its exits and entrances, its whole design along with all its statutes, forms, and laws. Write it down in their sight, so that they may keep its complete design and all its statutes and may carry them out.
This is the law of the temple: All its surrounding territory on top of the mountain will be most holy. Yes, this is the law of the temple.

These are the measurements of the altar in long cubits (a cubit and a handbreadth): Its gutter shall be a cubit deep and a cubit wide, with a rim of one span around its edge. And this is the height of the altar:

The space from the gutter on the ground to the lower ledge shall be two cubits, and the ledge one cubit wide. The space from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge shall be four cubits, and the ledge one cubit wide.
The altar hearth shall be four cubits high, and four horns shall project upward from the hearth.
The altar hearth shall be square at its four corners, twelve cubits long and twelve cubits wide.
The ledge shall also be square, fourteen cubits long and fourteen cubits wide, with a rim of half a cubit and a gutter of a cubit all around it. The steps of the altar shall face east.”

Then He said to me: “Son of man, this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘These are the statutes for the altar on the day it is constructed, so that burnt offerings may be sacrificed on it and blood may be sprinkled on it:
You are to give a young bull from the herd as a {{chatat|sin offering}} to the Levitical priests who are of the family of Zadok, who approach Me to minister before Me, declares the Lord GOD.

You are to take some of its blood and put it on the four horns of the altar, on the four corners of the ledge, and all around the rim; thus you will cleanse the altar and make {{kaphar|atonement}} for it.
Then you are to take away the bull for the sin offering and burn it in the appointed part of the temple area outside the sanctuary.
On the second day you are to present an unblemished male goat as a sin offering, and the altar is to be cleansed as it was with the bull.
When you have finished the purification, you are to present a young, unblemished bull and an unblemished ram from the flock.
You must present them before the LORD; the priests are to sprinkle salt on them and sacrifice them as a burnt offering to the LORD.
For seven days you are to provide a male goat daily for a sin offering; you are also to provide a young bull and a ram from the flock, both unblemished.
For seven days the priests are to make atonement for the altar and cleanse it; so they shall consecrate it.
At the end of these days, from the eighth day on, the priests are to present your burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar. Then I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD.’”

kavod.gloss: Glory, weight, the visible splendor of God's manifest presence. The very kavod that departed the temple in chapters 10-11 now returns from the east, filling the house exactly where it once stood empty.

shakan.gloss: To dwell, to settle down, to tabernacle. The root behind mishkan, tabernacle; here God promises to shakan, dwell, among His people forever, the goal toward which the whole measured vision has been moving.

chatat.gloss: Sin offering, purification offering. The sacrifice that cleanses the altar itself before it can be used, teaching that even the place of worship needs atonement before a holy God can be approached.

kaphar.gloss: To atone, to cover, to make propitiation. The verb behind Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement; here it describes cleansing the newly built altar itself, so that sacrifice can rightly begin upon it.

basic.context: This chapter is the turning point of the whole temple vision. In chapters 8-11 Ezekiel watched, in stages, the glory of the LORD leave a temple defiled by idolatry, pausing at the threshold before departing over the Mount of Olives. Now, after the measured house of chapters 40-42 stands ready though empty, that same glory returns, from the east, with a voice like many waters, and fills the temple completely. God declares this the place of His throne, promises to dwell there forever if His people put away their defilement, and then gives exact instructions for consecrating the altar so that atonement, and worship, can begin again.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter deliberately recalls Ezekiel's own earlier visions, 'like the vision I had seen when He came to destroy the city,' 43:3, so that readers feel the reversal: the glory that left in judgment now returns in mercy, following the very route it took away. As with the surrounding temple vision, interpreters differ on how literally to press the architectural and ritual detail, but the theological center is unmistakable: sin drives God's presence away, and only genuine repentance and atonement make His dwelling possible again.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter is built around kavod, glory, the same word used for the throne vision of chapter 1 and the departing glory of chapters 10-11, now returning. God promises to shakan, dwell, among His people forever, the very root behind the tabernacle's name. And the new altar must be cleansed by a chatat, sin offering, so that kaphar, atonement, can be made before ordinary worship begins.
basic.typology: The glory's return by the east gate anticipates a greater return: the eternal Word becoming flesh and tabernacling among us, John 1:14, the same root idea as shakan here. The altar's seven-day consecration by blood anticipates the once-for-all cleansing accomplished at the cross, after which no further consecration of an altar is ever needed.
basic.christ: John deliberately echoes this chapter's language when he writes that 'the Word became flesh and dwelt,' literally tabernacled, 'among us, and we have seen His glory,' John 1:14, the same kavod Ezekiel watched fill this temple. Where Ezekiel needed seven days of sacrifice to consecrate an altar, Hebrews says Christ 'entered once for all into the holy places... by means of His own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption,' Hebrews 9:12. The temple that received the glory back is fulfilled in the One who is Himself God with us, and who will one day be, with the Lamb, the temple of the new creation, Revelation 21:22-23.
basic.god: God is holy and cannot dwell amid ongoing defilement; His anger in chapters 8-11 was real and just. Yet He is a God whose settled intention is to dwell with His people, not to remain at a distance; the very first thing He says upon returning is a promise, 'I will dwell among them forever' (43:9), conditioned only on their putting away what drove Him out.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 10:18-19 and 11:22-23 describe the glory's earlier, grieving departure from this same temple and city, now reversed. John 1:14 identifies the same glory, tabernacling among us, in Christ. Hebrews 9:11-12 fulfills the altar's repeated consecration in Christ's once-for-all entrance by His own blood. Revelation 21:3 and 22 show God's dwelling finally and fully with man.
basic.oneStory: The Bible's story keeps circling one question: will God dwell with His people, or must He depart because of sin? Eden lost that presence; the tabernacle and temple recovered it in shadow; sin drove the glory out in Ezekiel's own lifetime; and here, that same glory returns, pointing beyond itself to Christ, in whom God's presence became permanent and unshakable, and to the new creation, where God dwells with His people forever, needing no temple at all because He is the temple.

context.literary:
Chapter 43 is built as a return journey that mirrors the departure of chapters 10 and 11, stage by stage. Then the glory moved from the cherubim's throne to the threshold, to the east gate, and finally rose from the city and stood over the mountain on the east, Ezekiel 10:18 and 19, 11:22 and 23. Now it comes the opposite way, from the east, to the east gate, through it and into the temple, 43:2 to 5. The departure took three halts and the return takes one, a single movement with no hesitation. The vision lines up by design with the chapter that grieves the loss.

The chapter has two halves with a hinge between them. In verses 1 to 9 the glory arrives and speaks. In verses 10 to 12 Ezekiel is told what to do with what he has seen, and in verses 13 to 27 the altar is measured and consecrated. Verse 12 sums up the middle, this is the law of the temple, with the repeated phrase, Yes, this is the law of the temple, a seal placed on the instruction. The whole mountain is most holy, so that holiness is no longer limited to a single room and spreads to the entire summit.

Within the first half the experience is sensory. The sound is like many waters, the earth shines, the prophet falls on his face, and then the Spirit lifts him up and sets him in the inner court, 43:2 to 5. Within the second half, by contrast, the style is flat and technical, with measurements, a sequence of animals, and a calendar of seven days. The two registers belong together, since the glory has come and the way of approach must now be fixed.
context.historical:
Ezekiel saw the glory leave in 592 BC, in the sixth year of the exile, and the city fell in 586 BC. The date of this vision is about 573 BC, so nineteen years had passed since the glory's last recorded appearance in Jerusalem. The exiles had learned a hard truth, which was that the presence of God could not be held by a building. The prophet Jeremiah had told them not to trust in the temple of the LORD as though the words were a charm, and chapter 8 of Ezekiel showed what had been done inside it.

The charges in 43:7 and 8 have a specific background. The kings had put their own threshold next to the LORD's and their doorposts beside His, with only a wall between. This is a reference to the way the palace stood beside the temple on the same hill, as Solomon's palace did, 1 Kings 7:1 to 12, so that the royal house and the holy house were one complex. When the kings practised idolatry and honored their own dead, the defilement reached the temple. The word the BSB translates as funeral offerings is uncertain, and the footnote offers monuments and a reading about the kings on their high places. In either case, the verse is about a royal cult that mixed with the worship of the LORD.

The altar of 43:13 to 17 is described in the long cubit, which the BSB footnote gives as about twenty one inches. The hearth is twelve cubits square, about twenty one feet, set on a fourteen cubit ledge, and the whole is four horned and reached by steps facing east. The Zadokite priests of 43:19 are the line that had kept charge of the sanctuary, as 44:15 says, and Zadok himself had been established as priest in the days of Solomon, 1 Kings 2:35.
context.canonical:
The glory that fills the house is a theme with a long history. The glory filled the tabernacle when Moses had finished it, Exodus 40:34 and 35, and filled Solomon's temple so that the priests could not stand to minister, 1 Kings 8:10 and 11. Ezekiel's own first vision of the glory by the river Chebar uses the same voice like many waters that is heard in 43:2, compare 1:24. After this return, 44:1 and 2 says the east gate must stay shut because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it.

Other prophets look for the same return. Malachi says the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple, Malachi 3:1. Haggai promises that the latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, Haggai 2:9, and Zechariah hears God say I am coming to dwell among you, Zechariah 2:10. Isaiah calls Zion to arise and shine because the glory of the LORD rises upon her, Isaiah 60:1 and 2.

The New Testament takes up the glory as a person. John says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen His glory, John 1:14. Hebrews calls the Son the radiance of God's glory, Hebrews 1:3, and Paul says God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, 2 Corinthians 4:6. The altar and its consecration are also taken up. Exodus 29:36 and 37 prescribes seven days of atonement for the altar, and Hebrews says the law is a shadow of good things to come, and that where sins have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed, Hebrews 10:1 and 18. Revelation 21:3 and 22 closes the line, with God's dwelling with man and no temple, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wanted the exiles to understand that the return of God's presence has a condition, and that the condition is moral, not architectural. The command in verse 9, now let them remove far from Me their prostitution and the funeral offerings for their kings, and I will dwell among them forever, joins a promise to a demand. The glory is not tied to the stones. It is tied to what the people do with the God who lives in the stones. A people who had assumed that the temple guaranteed God's favor were to learn that God Himself decides who may come near.

He also wanted them to feel the reversal of the earlier vision. The words like the vision I had seen when He came to destroy the city, 43:3, tell the exiles that the glory who judged is the same glory who restores. It is not a different God, and it is not a change of mind in the sense of a new character. The anger of chapter 8 to 11 and the welcome of chapter 43 come from the same holiness. A reader who has only known the stern chapters will find that the glory comes back by the very gate it left, and in the same splendor.

Finally, the chapter is meant to teach the exiles how to approach. The altar is measured and consecrated before any worship begins, because God has set a way for sinners to come near Him, and it is by atonement. The promise in verse 27, I will accept you, is the heart of that way, and it is what the prophet means his hearers to take away.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what Ezekiel saw and heard in a vision and sets out the rules for an altar in a temple that has not yet been built. It does not command anyone in Ezekiel's day or in ours to construct this altar or to offer these sacrifices. The instruction to Ezekiel is to describe the temple to the people so that they may be ashamed, 43:10, and the statutes for the altar are reported as what God says will apply on the day it is constructed, 43:18.

What is prescriptive in a lasting sense is the moral center. The people are to remove their idolatry, and holiness is to cover the whole area, 43:9 and 12. That is a principle that applies whenever God's people draw near to Him. The Christian reader is told that the church is God's temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 17, and so the demand to put away what defiles it has direct application.

On the altar and its sacrifices, the New Testament has given clear guidance about what the work of Christ means for the sacrificial system. Hebrews says that there is no longer an offering for sin where sin has been forgiven, 10:18. How that bears on the details of this chapter is a question on which sincere readers differ, and the chapter itself does not answer it. What it settles is that approach to God goes by way of atonement.

debates.question: Why does Ezekiel stress that this vision is like the vision by the River Kebar, 43:3?

views.label: To prove the glory is the same glory
views.case: The prophet has seen the glory three times, at the river in chapter 1, in the temple in chapters 8 to 11, and now here. By tying them together he assures the reader that the God who left is the God who returns, and that this is no lesser appearance.

views.label: To show judgment and restoration are one work
views.case: The vision when He came to destroy the city is placed between the other two. In this reading the verse says that the one who judged in Jerusalem is also the one who restores, and that both come from His holiness.

views.label: A textual question about who destroyed
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that some Hebrew manuscripts and the Vulgate read when I came to destroy the city, where most Hebrew manuscripts read as the BSB does. On that reading the prophet himself is pictured as coming to destroy, in the sense of announcing it, as prophets sometimes do. The theological result is the same.

debates.bearing: All three are compatible. The verse binds the three visions into one story, and it shows that the glory who returns is the glory who left, now coming in mercy.

debates.question: Do the altar and its sacrifices anticipate a future, literal reinstitution of animal offerings?

views.label: A literal future temple with sacrifices as memorials
views.case: The text gives exact instructions for sacrifices, and the prophecy is set in the age of the restoration. Some readers hold that animal offerings will return in the kingdom as remembrance of Christ's finished work, as the Lord's Supper looks back to it now.

views.label: A picture of worship in the language of the Old Testament
views.case: Prophets describe the future in the forms of their own day. On this reading the altar and the sacrifices are Ezekiel's way of saying that the people will worship fully and that atonement stands at the center. Hebrews 10:1 to 4 and 18 shows that the shadows are fulfilled in Christ.

views.label: A conditional pattern that was not carried out
views.case: The statutes are given on the condition of the people's repentance, 43:10 and 11. If the pattern was an offer to a returning people, its details were never applied as written.

debates.bearing: Each view takes seriously the book of Hebrews, which says the sacrifices cannot finish what they signify, and each takes seriously what Ezekiel writes. What the chapter plainly says is that atonement comes before acceptance, and this remains true.

debates.question: Is the promise to dwell forever conditional?

views.label: Conditional on the people
views.case: Verse 9 says let them remove their idolatry, and I will dwell among them forever. The presence depends on the response, as it did when the glory left.

views.label: Secured by God
views.case: Verse 7 says the place is where I will dwell among the Israelites forever, and the surrounding chapters, 37:26 to 28, state an everlasting covenant. The condition describes what the people will do when He makes them new, 36:26 and 27.

debates.bearing: Ezekiel holds both. The demand is real, and the promise is certain because God Himself will bring about what He demands, as chapter 36 shows.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with the description of the sound in 43:2, His voice was like the roar of many waters, in Hebrew qol mayim rabbim. The same simile is used in 1:24 of the sound of the creatures' wings, and the Hebrew idiom means a great, rushing noise, like the sea. It is not the whisper of 1 Kings 19. That the earth shone with His glory, in the same verse, links the sound with light, and it is an echo of the throne vision.

The word the BSB renders as prostitution in 43:7 and 9 is zenut, the term for faithless idolatry that Ezekiel uses throughout, in chapter 16 and chapter 23. The word it renders as funeral offerings is uncertain, and the BSB offers monuments in a footnote. The effect is the same, since the charge is that the royal house has set up a rival to the LORD's own honor. The language of threshold and doorpost, 43:8, is one of closeness, with only a wall between Me and them, and it makes the sin an offence against nearness.

The command in verse 10 uses the verb kalam, to be ashamed or humiliated. God wants the people to be brought to a felt, honest shame, and the measurement of the plan is to be the means. The statement in verse 12, this is the law of the temple, uses torah, the same word as the law of Moses. It is not a rule about how the building is to be made but a teaching about what the place is. The summit is most holy, qodesh qodashim, and it is the holiness of the Most Holy Place that is now extended over the whole mountaintop.

The verb in 43:20 and 22 that the BSB renders cleanse is chitte, a form that is built from the word for sin and means to de-sin, to purify from sin. It is the verb for what the blood does to the altar. Then in verse 26, the BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew behind consecrate is literally fill its hand. This is the idiom used for the ordination of priests, as in Leviticus 8:33, so the altar is ordained like a priest, as it were, by seven days of atonement.

The last word is ratsah, accept, in verse 27, I will accept you. It is the word used for a sacrifice that is received with favor, and here it is promised to the worshiper himself. The eighth day is the day when the offerings begin, and the acceptance is spoken to the people. The whole process is to open a way to be welcomed.

typology.type: The glory entering by the east gate, Ezekiel 43:1-5
typology.fulfillment: The return of the glory is the type of the coming of God to dwell with His people. John says the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us, and we have seen His glory, John 1:14, and Malachi's promise that the Lord will suddenly come to His temple, Malachi 3:1, is taken up in the gospel story. Jesus entered Jerusalem from the east, from the Mount of Olives, Luke 19:37 and 45. The type is exceeded because the glory comes in a human body, and it goes further than a building to fill a people.

typology.type: The place of My throne and the soles of My feet, Ezekiel 43:7
typology.fulfillment: God declares that this place is His throne and the resting place for His feet, among the Israelites forever. The New Testament says the exalted Christ is seated at the right hand of the throne, Hebrews 8:1, and that the throne of God and of the Lamb stands in the city, Revelation 22:3. The type falls short because it is bound to one site, while the throne of grace is open to all who draw near, Hebrews 4:16.

typology.type: The altar of burnt offering with its horns and ledges, Ezekiel 43:13-17
typology.fulfillment: The altar is the place where atonement is made, and its horns are touched with blood, 43:20. Christ is the one who has entered once for all by His own blood, Hebrews 9:12, and Hebrews 13:10 to 12 says we have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. The type is fulfilled and exceeded, since it needed repeating and the cross does not.

typology.type: The seven days of consecration with sin offerings, Ezekiel 43:18-27
typology.fulfillment: The altar is cleansed with a bull and a goat before it is used, much as Exodus 29:36 and 37 prescribes seven days for the first altar. The pattern says that even the place of atonement must be atoned for. Hebrews says Christ, unlike those priests, has no need to offer sacrifices daily for His own sins and then for the people, for He did it once for all when He offered Himself, Hebrews 7:27. The type falls short because the altar had to be purified, while Christ is the pure and sinless offering.

typology.type: The law of the temple, all the summit most holy, Ezekiel 43:12
typology.fulfillment: The extension of holiness from the inner room to the whole mountain points to a people and a place wholly holy. Paul says that God's temple is holy and that the church is that temple, 1 Corinthians 3:17, and Peter calls believers a holy priesthood, 1 Peter 2:5. The vision comes to its end in a city where nothing unclean enters, Revelation 21:27. The type falls short because the holiness is still guarded by walls.

study.christ:
Ezekiel 43 leads to Christ along the line of glory, the line of the altar, and the line of the people, and the three meet in one verse of John. The first line is glory. In chapter 43 the glory of the God of Israel comes to the temple from the east, and the earth shines, and the house is filled. John writes that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen His glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, John 1:14. The verb John chooses, to tabernacle, belongs to the same family of ideas as the dwelling of 43:7 and 9, I will dwell among them forever. Paul can say that God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, 2 Corinthians 4:6, and Hebrews calls the Son the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His being, Hebrews 1:3. What Ezekiel saw come toward a building has come in a person.

The second line is the altar. The chapter turns directly from the glory to the way of approach, because the glory cannot dwell among people without atonement. Seven days of sin offerings, blood on the horns, the bull burned outside, the goat, the ram, all must happen before the altar is used and the people can be accepted, 43:27. Hebrews answers this. The law is a shadow of good things to come, and its repeated sacrifices could never make perfect those who draw near, Hebrews 10:1. Christ went in a single time into the true sanctuary, taking His own blood and not the blood of goats and calves, Hebrews 9:12. He is both the priest and the offering. The animal burned outside the sanctuary in 43:21 lies behind the statement that Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through His own blood, Hebrews 13:11 and 12. Where Ezekiel's text says I will accept you, 43:27, the New Testament says that we have been accepted in the Beloved, Ephesians 1:6.

The third line is the people. The glory fills the house and the altar opens the way, and then the temple is no longer a building but a body of people. Paul tells the Corinthians that they are the temple of the living God and that God's Spirit dwells in them, 1 Corinthians 3:16. The condition of verse 9, to put away the defilement, is met in Christ, who has cleansed us and who works in us by the Spirit, as chapter 36 promised.

We should be careful not to make each measurement of the altar a picture of Christ. The ledges, the horns and the steps are the language of the Old Testament altar and need no allegory. The link is in the movement, the glory returns, atonement is made, God accepts and dwells. That movement is completed in Christ, who is the glory, the sacrifice and the priest, and who will one day be the temple itself with the Father, Revelation 21:22.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God whose anger and love are not in conflict. The glory who left in judgment returns in mercy, and the vision says plainly that they are the same, like the vision I had seen when He came to destroy the city, 43:3. His anger in chapters 8 to 11 was real, and verse 8 recalls it, I have consumed them in My anger. But anger was never His last word. This is a God whose settled purpose is to live among His people, and who will not be put off by their failure or kept from His purpose by their sin.

He is holy, and He is the one who determines how He is approached. The altar must be cleansed before any offering is made, and the seven days of atonement come before the day of acceptance. This is not a bureaucratic detail. It shows that holiness is not a feeling or a mood but a standard, and that the God of Israel does not overlook sin to be near. Yet in the same chapter He is the one who provides the way, giving the instructions and promising acceptance. He asks for atonement and He gives the means.

He is a God who speaks from within His house. In verse 6 Ezekiel hears someone speaking to him from inside the temple, and the voice declares this is the place of My throne and the place for the soles of My feet. The God who sits enthroned in glory is also the God who puts His feet on the ground among His people. Isaiah 66:1 says heaven is His throne and earth His footstool, and here He takes a particular place on the earth. The transcendent God is also near.

He is a God who tells the truth about His people. He names their prostitution and the funeral offerings for their kings, and He does so so that they may be ashamed. This is not cruelty, since shame is the beginning of repentance. A God who loves people tells them what has gone wrong.

He is a God who is faithful to what He has promised. The promise to dwell forever, verse 7, belongs with the covenant of peace and the sanctuary set among them forever in 37:26 to 28. He does not change, and what He has said He will do.

For worship, the chapter calls us to come near with both joy and reverence. The same God who is a consuming fire welcomes sinners by atonement, and the right response to a glory that has returned is to fall facedown, as Ezekiel did, and then to be lifted by the Spirit and set on our feet in His house, 43:3 and 5.

crossReferences.note: The glory of the LORD moves from the threshold of the temple and stops at the entrance of the east gate. This is the first stage of the departure that chapter 43 reverses, with the glory coming in by the same east gate.
The glory rises from within the city and stands over the mountain east of the city. The glory's last recorded place before the exile is the starting point from which it returns in 43:2.
The sound of the wings is like the roar of many waters, like the voice of the Almighty. The same sound accompanies the glory in 43:2, which ties the return to the throne vision at the river Chebar.
The east gate is to remain shut because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it. The chapter that follows records the lasting effect of the glory's entrance, a gate sealed by His passing.

The cloud covers the tent of meeting and the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle, so that Moses cannot enter. The glory that fills the temple in Ezekiel 43:5 is the same that filled the first sanctuary at Sinai.

When the priests came out of the holy place, the cloud filled the house of the LORD, and they could not stand to minister because of the glory. Ezekiel 43 is the answer to the loss of that glory in Solomon's house.

For seven days the priests are to make atonement for the altar and consecrate it, so that the altar becomes most holy. The seven day pattern of Ezekiel 43:25 and 26 follows this older rule for the first altar.
The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple. Malachi, writing after the exile, still looks for a coming of God that the second temple had not yet seen, and the Gospels take it up.
The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, and in this place God will give peace. Haggai speaks to the rebuilt temple and promises the glory that Ezekiel saw returning.
The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen His glory. John uses the vocabulary of the tent and of glory to say that the presence Ezekiel saw come to the temple has come in a person.

Christ entered the greater and more perfect tent and went once for all into the holy places by His own blood, securing an eternal redemption. This answers the seven days and the repeated blood of Ezekiel 43:18 to 27.
A loud voice from the throne says that the dwelling of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. This is the final form of the promise in Ezekiel 43:7 and 9, I will dwell among them forever.

study.oneStory:
The question that runs under the whole Bible is whether God will live with His people. In Eden He walked in the garden in the breeze of the day, and then the man and woman hid, and the way to the tree of life was barred. In the tabernacle and the temple the question was answered by a sanctuary and a sacrifice, and the glory filled the house. In Ezekiel's day sin drove the glory away, and the exile was the visible sign of the answer no. Chapter 43 gives the opposite word. The glory returns, by the same road it left, and fills the house, and God says that this is the place of His throne and the place for the soles of His feet, where He will dwell forever.

The chapter does not allow the return to be cheap. The first thing that follows it is a consecrated altar. The story has taught from Genesis 4 and Exodus 29 that a holy God is approached by way of blood, and this passage ties the return of the glory to a sin offering for the very place where worship takes place. Even the altar must be cleansed. This is the shape of the whole biblical answer, presence by way of atonement, and it is how a holy God can live with a sinful people.

The chapter sets up the next part of the book. In 44:1 and 2 the east gate is sealed, and in chapters 45 and 46 the prince, the priests and the feasts take their places. In chapter 47 the river flows out from the threshold, and the book ends in 48:35 with the name of the city, The LORD is there. The return of the glory is the turning point of the last section of Ezekiel, and the later chapters unfold what it means to live where God lives.

The New Testament says how the promise is kept. The Word becomes flesh and the glory is seen in Christ. The one sacrifice for sins is made, and the altar need not be consecrated again. The Spirit makes the church a temple, and the people who were far off are brought near. The Bible ends with the voice from the throne, the dwelling of God is with man, Revelation 21:3, in a city that has no temple because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, 21:22, and where the glory of God gives it light, 21:23. What Ezekiel saw from the east gate is the first sight of the end of the story, a house filled with glory and a people who are home.

quiz.q: From which direction does the glory of the LORD return to the temple?

options.text: From the west, over the Mediterranean
options.note: The text specifies a different direction.

options.text: From the north, through the idol gate
options.note: The idol gate is significant elsewhere in Ezekiel's visions, but the glory here returns from the east.

options.text: The text does not specify a direction
options.note: 43:2 and 43:4 are explicit that the glory comes from, and enters through, the east.

options.text: From the east, the same direction from which it had departed
options.note: 43:2 and 43:4 state this clearly, reversing the earlier departure over the Mount of Olives to the east.

quiz.q: What does God call this place in 43:7?

options.text: A monument to Israel's disobedience
options.note: The emphasis is on future dwelling and promise, not a monument to past failure.

options.text: The place of My throne and the place for the soles of My feet, where I will dwell forever
options.note: 43:7 records this declaration in almost these exact words.

options.text: A place He refuses to dwell in again
options.note: The opposite is stated; God promises to dwell there forever.

options.text: A temporary resting place until the next exile
options.note: The promise given is permanence, 'forever,' not a temporary arrangement.

quiz.q: What is Ezekiel commanded to do in 43:10-11?

options.text: Keep the vision completely secret from the people
options.note: He is told to describe it to the people, not conceal it.

options.text: Destroy the vision's plans because Israel is unworthy
options.note: He is told to record and make known the design, not destroy it.

options.text: Build the temple with his own hands immediately
options.note: He is commanded to describe and record the design, not to build it himself.

options.text: Describe the temple's design to Israel so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities and keep its statutes
options.note: 43:10-11 gives this exact commission.

quiz.q: What must happen to the altar before it can be used for regular offerings?

options.text: It must be moved to a different location outside the temple
options.note: No relocation is described; it must be cleansed in place.

options.text: It must be left unused for seven years
options.note: The consecration period given is seven days, not seven years.

options.text: It must be cleansed and consecrated over seven days through sin offerings and atoning blood
options.note: 43:18-27 describes this seven-day consecration in detail.

options.text: Nothing; it is ready for use immediately upon completion
options.note: The text describes a required seven-day process of cleansing before ordinary use begins.

quiz.q: What does God promise conditionally in 43:9, if Israel removes its former defilement?

options.text: That He will send them into exile one more time
options.note: The promise given is dwelling, not further exile.

options.text: That He will withdraw and never return
options.note: The whole chapter is about His return and promised presence, the opposite of withdrawal.

options.text: That He will destroy the temple again
options.note: The chapter's entire momentum is toward permanent dwelling, not further destruction.

options.text: That He will dwell among them forever
options.note: 43:9 states this promise directly, conditioned on removing the former defilement.

questions: The glory returns by the very gate it once departed through. Where in your own life might you need to trust that God can return to, and restore, places you thought were permanently lost to sin?

God says He will dwell with His people 'forever' only once they remove what defiled His name (43:9). How does the gospel's promise of full acceptance in Christ meet, rather than remove, the call to genuine repentance?

Ezekiel is told to describe the temple so Israel would be 'ashamed of their iniquities' (43:10). Is there a place where a clearer picture of God's holiness, rather than mere information, would produce healthy shame and real change in you?

The altar itself needed seven days of cleansing before it could be used for ordinary worship. How does knowing that even the place of sacrifice needed atonement deepen your appreciation for Christ's finished, once-for-all sacrifice?

John says Christ 'tabernacled' among us, using the very word behind God's promise to dwell with Israel here. How does picturing Jesus as this chapter's fulfillment change the way you approach Him in worship this week?

translationNotes.note: 'The vision I saw was like the vision I had seen when He came to destroy the city' deliberately links this scene back to the departure visions of chapters 8-11 and the inaugural vision of chapter 1, using closely parallel language so the reader recognizes the very same glory now returning.

'The soles of My feet' is a striking image, likely describing the temple, or the ark within it, as God's footstool, a picture used elsewhere for the earthly point of contact with a heavenly throne, compare 1 Chronicles 28:2 and Psalm 132:7.

'The Levitical priests of the family of Zadok' repeats a qualification given earlier in the vision, 40:46, restricting altar service to a specific priestly line, a detail read by some as a literal future arrangement and by others as a picture of a fully qualified, wholly consecrated priesthood.
